growth_story.headline: Jamaica spent decades under heavy debt; after a hard-won reset, income per person hit a record in 2023, two years before Hurricane Melissa struck.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Jamaica grew 1.2 percent a year from 1990 to 2007, an era the IMF links to a 1996 banking crisis whose rescue added heavily to public debt. From 2008 to 2015 it shrank by 0.8 percent a year, including a 4.7 percent fall in 2009, while a 2010 IMF-backed program went off track and debt stayed very high. A new program in 2013 began more than a decade of large budget surpluses that cut public debt, and growth recovered to 1.4 percent a year in 2016–2025, despite an 8.5 percent fall in 2020 when the pandemic hit tourism hard. In 2022 income per person passed its 1972 level for the first time, and in 2023 it reached the highest level on record. It then slipped after storms in 2024, and by 2025 it was 0.4 percent below the 2023 peak, with Hurricane Melissa striking in October 2025. The World Bank calls growth modest despite this progress, and lists low productivity, crime and informality among the long-running drags.

threads.title: A banking crisis and heavy debt
threads.text: The IMF traces Jamaica's long stretch of weak growth to a cycle of deficits and debt. A banking crisis broke out in 1996; a blanket deposit guarantee restored stability, but the rescue added a large share of a year's output to public debt, and high interest costs followed for more than a decade.

threads.text: For more than a decade Jamaica ran large budget surpluses and cut public debt sharply, which the World Bank says strengthened policy credibility. That stronger fiscal position framed the 2016–2025 recovery, and the World Bank says it helped cushion the 2025 hurricane.

since_last_year.text: Hurricane Melissa struck in October 2025 and reversed the recovery. The fiscal rules were suspended to pay for relief and rebuilding, the IMF approved an emergency disbursement in January 2026, and output fell sharply in early 2026. The World Bank expects the economy to shrink in 2026 and recover through reconstruction after that.

growth_story.tension: The annual data end in 2025 and show income per person only 0.4 percent below its 2023 peak, which reads as a small dip. The sources describe a much larger shock: Hurricane Melissa struck late in 2025, the IMF calls the destruction unprecedented, and the World Bank expects the economy to shrink in 2026. Most of that hit falls after the last year in the data.
